blocks.x: The emergency call alerting police to what might quite reasonably be labeled Tiger Woods’s Fourth Great Automotive Disaster came at 1:17 p.m. on March 27, 2026, from the super-high-end exclusively residential neighborhood of Florida’s Jupiter Island. An accident involving two vehicles had taken place on South Beach Road, the two-lane route running north-south up the thin barrier island’s center, separating homes on the bay from homes on the ocean.

In the aftermath of the day’s events, facing serious legal charges, Woods would issue a brief statement and enter a written plea of not guilty. Otherwise, he said nothing about the crash. His spokesperson did not respond to requests for comment, and his lawyer, when reached by GQ, said he does not discuss pending cases.

But the copious police body-camera footage from the scene plays out every strange, unexpected beat of that day’s aftermath. It offers a grippingly vivid glimpse of the remote life of one of the finest sportsmen we have ever known, whose cyclical downfalls and triumphant returns have, more times than almost seems possible, been punctuated by a moment when a police officer approaches his wrecked car.

A black Range Rover lies on its side, blocking one lane of the road. Its rear-window wiper goes pointlessly back and forth, back and forth, under the hot midday sun. Officer Anthony Fusco of the Jupiter Island Public Safety Department, just arriving, asks a man standing in the road, whose blue shirt identifies him as an employee of a local construction company, whether anyone is still in the car.

“No…he’s out,” says the man. The construction worker pulled up here just after the accident happened and helped the Range Rover’s driver clamber out of the passenger side door, the one facing up to the sky.
“Who’s involved?” asks Fusco.
What Fusco seems to mean by this is: Which of the people now on the scene were involved in the crash? But the man in the road answers his question in a slightly different way.
To do so, he lowers his voice almost to a whisper.
“Tiger Woods,” he says.
Who knows exactly what carousel of thoughts this information brings to Officer Fusco’s mind? All we can know for sure are the first two words that escape from his mouth in response.
“Oh shit,” he says.

As often as the capsule tale of Tiger Woods’s first rise is repeated, it never becomes any less improbable. He appeared on television playing golf at the age of two, already a prodigy, having learned to play by watching his father in their California garage. Whether propelled or guided by his father, at every stage of his youth Woods appeared to be better than anyone had ever been before him. By the time he turned professional, at 20 years old, he was already one of the most famous people in the country.

Whatever pressure all that expectation placed upon him, he delivered. For the next decade, golf was his. By age 32, he had won 14 majors. There was but one obvious remaining target ahead of him to cement his eternal greatness: Jack Nicklaus’s record of 18 majors. But Woods was comfortably ahead of schedule—by the same age Nicklaus had won 11—and it was surely just a question of time.
As though life, even for the greatest of us, ever remains that straightforward.

Tiger Woods, in a shimmering blue shirt, dark shorts, black cap, and mirrored sunglasses, is kneeling with his right leg on the grass on the side of the road, while Officer Christopher Trajbar, also from the Jupiter Island Public Safety Department, puts on disposable black gloves before carefully feeling his way up and down Woods’s back. Having seen Woods’s overturned car, a few feet away, Trajbar knows what to expect in accidents like these. In particular, to look for kinds of physical damage that the damaged may not yet have noticed. As Trajbar will later explain to a colleague: “I could have sworn there would have been glass or something in his back.”
But, to Trajbar’s surprise, there’s nothing. Woods has, in this way at least, been lucky.

Over in his car, Fusco is on the police radio, updating someone on the unexpected situation that has presented itself: “Hey—it’s Tiger. I just need you over here, just because of the sensitivity of it. He’s the one who rolled over.” Meanwhile, Trajbar walks a few yards southward down the road and approaches another man, this one standing by a truck, a trailer behind it. This is who, and what, Woods hit before his car turned onto its side. A horizontal sign running along the side of the trailer loudly advertises the man’s calling: JEROMY BULLARD’S CLEANING SERVICES. Soft Wash Roof Cleaning. Exterior Wall Cleaning. Driveway & Patio Cleaning. Paver & Deck Sealing.
“I was getting ready to turn….” Bullard begins, and explains what happened, an account he will relate multiple times over the next hour or so.

Bullard was driving north, heading for his next job at 281 South Beach Road. As he neared the home’s driveway, he put on his right turn signal and began to brake. But in his mirrors he could see a car on the road behind him, and as it came closer and closer, he realized that the car wasn’t slowing down. “He didn’t see me,” Bullard says, “and he just kept coming.” Bullard tried to pull over as far as he could, but it wasn’t enough. The right side of the fast-approaching car hit the driver’s side fender of his trailer (presumably because the car swerved, too late, at the very last minute). Continuing past him, the car pitched onto its side and slid along the road.

As the questions keep coming, Bullard answers them as best he can. Asked how fast Woods was driving, he replies that he can’t tell. “I mean, I don’t think it was crazy. It was normal speed. I just don’t know what was going on…he might have just not saw me. I don’t know. That’s the only thing I can think of.”
And what, he is asked, were your observations of him when he got out of the vehicle? (Bullard also helped Woods from his car.)
“He seemed okay….”
Apologetic, or…?

“I think he was just…he was like, ‘Oh shit.’ I think he was just flustered. He lives just down there. I know him…you know, I know who he is. I’m sure it’s”—Bullard offers a kind of half laugh—“not something that he just wanted to have happen. I didn’t want it to happen. Especially by him. You know? You know what I mean?”
Officer Fusco arranges for Woods to sit in the back seat of a police car, a few yards down the driveway to Hobe Sound Yacht Club, so that he can be somewhat out of the way.
“Are you alright?” Fusco asks. “Are you in any pain?”
“No,” says Woods. “No. No pain.”
“No back pain? No neck pain?”
“No.”
“Knee?”
“Nope.”
“Nothing?” Fusco reconfirms.
It is only now that Woods offers what may come to be seen as an important clarification.
“Nothing unusual,” he says.

The single most obvious reason why, after 2008, Woods’s career faltered so badly relates to the daunting series of physical setbacks he faced: cartilage damage, torn ACL, pinched nerve, back spasms and pain, sciatica, scar tissue. Over the next decade, he would undergo four back surgeries and three knee surgeries (totaling five), and his career seemed a stuttering catalog of rehabs, comebacks, and setbacks. Some commentators wondered about his instinct to play through pain and his tendency to return too soon. Also about his drive to put on upper body mass, and his unusual choice to leverage his celebrity to train with Navy SEALs. But Woods, looking back, would argue that his injuries were simply the consequence of pushing his body so hard for so long to be the best: “That’s just the wear and tear of doing my sport, of just trying to push it to win everything I possibly can. To win every single tournament I played in, I would do everything I possibly could. Like any sport, there’s a cost to it. There’s a cost of doing business and, unfortunately, for sportsmen and sportswomen, injuries are a part of it.”

They hit him hard. By the end of 2017, Woods, who had once cumulatively topped the weekly golf rankings for over 10 years, dropped out of the top one thousand. Though he kept pushing, kept coming back to the tour, it seemed rational to believe that his time as a competitor at the highest level was all but over.

Not long after the first responders arrive, Woods is joined by two people from his world. One, wearing a green shirt with a Smith & Wesson logo on its back, is part of the security detail stationed at Woods’s home two miles down the road, though from the conversations he has with the local officers it’s clear that he previously used to be one of them. The second, in a blue-and-white striped shirt from Woods’s golfwear merchandise line, Sun Day Red, is Rob McNamara, vice president of Woods’s company, TGR Ventures, though law enforcement will refer to him as Woods’s manager. He and Woods have known each other since they both played junior golf, and he has worked with, and been friends with, Woods for a quarter of a century. Business aside, Woods has long trusted him as an adviser on the mechanics of Woods’s game.
When Fusco talks with McNamara about the tow truck on its way that will right, and then remove, Woods’s car, McNamara alerts him to one particular priority: “It’s just the clubs.”
“Yeah, no, I understand,” says Fusco. “Worth more than my house.”
“The putter’s worth more than all of our houses,” McNamara says.

A few minutes later a new figure on the scene, Sheriff Deputy Brenovil of the Martin County Sheriff’s Department, introduces himself to Woods and explains that he will be doing the accident investigation. He asks Woods what happened.
This is how Woods explains it: “Yeah, I was looking down at my phone, looked at changing stations, and next thing I was…boom!”

The strange thing about the way Woods says this is that there’s no apparent acknowledgment or sense that he fucked up. Maybe he considers it simply too obvious to state. But it’s also true that you could easily listen to him talking here and get the impression that what he’s actually saying is: I was looking at my phone and changing radio stations and all the normal things you do when you’re driving, and suddenly the world played an unfair trick on me.
After Brenovil concludes this first conversation and walks away, Fusco asks Woods: “Other than the clubs, is there anything else in there that you absolutely need at the moment?”
“No,” says Woods. “Just the sticks.”
“‘Just the sticks’—okay,” repeats Fusco. After some more chat back and forth, he asks, “Is that putter just the one you’ve taken with your career, or what?”
“Uh,” says Woods, “I’ve won 14 majors with it.”
“With that putter?” says Fusco.
“Yeah,” says Woods.
“Wow,” says Fusco. “They didn’t call you the GOAT for nothing, man.”
Woods doesn’t visibly react to this sentence, though it’s hard not to wonder whether what he heard loudest was the intended compliment or Fusco’s use of the past tense.

“That one club,” McNamara says. “There’s only one other club that’s won more majors than that individual club. Jack had one, like, 3-wood or something.” (Jack Nicklaus used the same MacGregor Tommy Armour 3-wood between 1958 and 1995, including during all of his 18 major titles.)
Fusco turns back to Woods.
“Are you golfing in the Masters this year?”
“Hoping to,” says Woods, evenly.
“Depends on y’all,” mutters the green-shirted security man.

In the long decade after Woods’s 14th major victory, in 2008, as he kept coming back, kept trying, it was as though he believed something was possible that few other people did. Thing is, he was right. Improbably, after everything, in April 2019, his game having cohered for a while and his body holding together, he achieved one further triumph: winning the Masters, his 15th major. Coming off the 18th green, after one final stroke with that famous putter (this its 14th victory, because his very first had been with another), one of the first people he hugged after his family was McNamara.

And Woods is trying, still. He never explicitly states where he was heading in the car today before this accident, but the circumstantial evidence suggests he was off to the golf course. His clubs are in the car; the local golf course he has been known to play at, Medalist, is in the direction he was going; and at one point today, as they wait, he says to McNamara, “So much for hitting balls today.”

Three days earlier, Woods had played for his Jupiter Links team in the new TGL team golf league he has been an instrumental part of creating: a format which uses a hybrid of a golf simulator for long shots and real putting surfaces. It was the first true competitive game of any kind Woods had played since the previous February, his most recent surgeries having been for a ruptured left Achilles tendon in March 2025 and a disc replacement surgery on his spine that October. Nonetheless, in the press conference after Jupiter Links’ loss that night, when Woods was asked whether he might play in the Masters, only two weeks away, he’d made clear that he wasn’t yet ruling it out.

“I’ve been trying,” he said. “This body, it doesn’t recover like it was when I was 24, 25. It doesn’t mean I’m not trying. I’ve been trying for a while…I keep trying. I want to play…I’ll be practicing playing at home this week, and keep trying to make progress.”
That, presumably, is what today, until things went wrong, was for. He was trying. By now, though, he was dealing with more than just the physical damage caused by all his years of golf.
Tiger’s Car Crash Timeline
Woods has a history of dangerous incidents while behind the wheel. None led to death or injuries, save the ones that Woods sustained.
Tiger Woods’s Third Great Automotive Disaster

On February 22, 2021, Tiger Woods was playing golf at Rolling Hills Country Club, just south of Los Angeles, a course he hadn’t returned to since his junior golf tournament days. (When, naturally, he had won; the prize back then was a boom box.) After the 2019 Masters win, Woods’s career had resumed its stop-start trajectory—a fifth knee operation, then a brief hot streak going into 2020 before his body had once more rebelled. Now Woods was nursing himself back into competitive form after his fifth back operation, a microdiscectomy, though that day he was being filmed by Friday Night Lights director Peter Berg as he offered golfing instruction to three celebrities: Dwyane Wade, David Spade, and Jada Pinkett-Smith.

In return, Pinkett-Smith in particular—who told him she started taking golf seriously in 2019 after her husband called and told her to turn the TV on during the final round of the Masters because “Tiger’s about to make history”—got him to open up a little.
At one point, when he seemed to be implying that he just can’t do everything in quite the same way as he once could, and then said, “Sucks when you’re older,” she pushed back.
“I like the wisdom that comes with it,” she said.
“Yeah, but…” he retorted.
“The body?” she asked.
“But the body…” he said.

A while later, when he picked up this thought—“You’re right about the wisdom part of it but…the body. I’ve had 10 operations”—she countered by telling him that it’s so inspiring what he’s overcome. Woods seemed bemused and embarrassed by this.
“I just don’t look at it like that,” he said.
“Well, you should,” she told him.
“But I don’t know how to,” he responded.
“Tiger,” she said, “your journey has been absolutely amazing.”
“Hmmm,” he said.
“It has been amazing,” she repeated.
“I just don’t see it that way,” Woods said.
“One day you will,” she told him.
“I don’t think so,” he said. He was smiling, almost bashful, but shaking his head. “I don’t look at it like that.”
“You should,” she persisted.
“I know,” he said. “I just look at the fight.”
This didn’t sound like banter. It sounded as though, caught off guard by someone he respected, Woods couldn’t think of anything to say but the truth.

They shared one more particularly noteworthy exchange, as they walked across the course down toward a lake. Pinkett-Smith explained that golf is a new kind of challenge for her because she’s never been a particularly disciplined person and she’s never had to work that hard at much.
“You feel like you’ve, like, have gotten away with just talent?” asked Woods.
“Yes,” she said.

“For me,” he said, “I always thought I wasn’t the most talented. So I felt like I had to work my ass off. Because I was always younger than everyone else…so I wanted to become, like, better…. I was always small…I wasn’t, like, the best at what I did.”

It’s a mesmerizing exchange. In part, for Woods’s demeanor, more honest and thoughtful and real than the stilted, awkward, punchier persona he often presents to the world. But it is also fascinating for the context it offers to what would happen next. When things go wrong in Tiger Woods’s world—and they were once more about to do so—such events are sometimes depicted as evidence that Woods has long been lost in an unsafe, self-destructive hazy spiral. Even if there are ways in which that might be so, this taping with Pinkett-Smith is a snapshot of how Woods was only hours before it all went wrong again: open, lucid, vulnerable, and in all obvious ways, entirely together.

The next morning, Woods was due back at Rolling Hills for more filming. New celebrity tutees, Drew Brees and Justin Herbert, would be waiting. Just before seven o’clock, Woods picked up his car from the valet at the Terranea Resort where he was staying and headed off. Just over halfway to his destination, as he drove down Hawthorne Boulevard, his Genesis SUV failed to follow the curve of the road. Instead, it, and Woods, traveled straight on, first hitting the central meridian and smashing through the large wooden sign announcing “Welcome to Rolling Hills Estates,” then crossing the two lanes of traffic in the opposite direction, before plowing into shrubbery, uprooting a tree, and finally coming to rest on its side. The car’s inbuilt event-data-recorder system would suggest that his vehicle had been traveling at over 80 miles an hour (the speed limit was 45) and offered no indication that the brakes were applied before the crash.

The first person on the scene, a local resident, found Woods unconscious. Deputy Carlos Gonzalez of the LA County Sheriff’s office, who arrived soon afterward, observed that Woods’s vehicle had “massive front end damage” and later told the news media: “I’ve seen fatal traffic collisions, so I will say it’s very fortunate that Mr. Woods was able to come out of this.”

In the trauma bay at Harbor-UCLA hospital, a police investigator interviewed Woods (referred to in his report as P-1): “P-1 told me he did not remember being involved in a traffic collision. P-1 thought he was currently in the state of Florida.” As the investigator and Woods spoke, a deep laceration on the right side of his jaw was being stitched, but it was his leg and foot injuries that were far more serious. The surgeon soon offered an update: “Comminuted open fractures affecting both the upper and lower portions of the tibia and fibula bones were stabilized by inserting a rod into the tibia. Additional injuries to the bones of the foot and ankle were stabilized with a combination of screws and pins. Trauma to the muscle and soft tissue of the leg required surgical release of the covering of the muscles to relieve pressure due to swelling.”

Amputation, Woods revealed eight months later, had been on the table. He spent three weeks in the hospital and more than two more months at home in Jupiter Island in a hospital bed. He talked about what a milestone it was when he could first be wheeled outdoors in the Florida sun, and how he eventually could use crutches. “I’d built a really nice house,” he observed, “but I didn’t realize how big it was until you start putting crutches on.”

When interviewed on the day of the crash, Woods denied having drunk alcohol or taken prescription medication either the previous night or that morning, and no testing was done which contradicted his assertions. The police report offered the opinion that Woods was at fault for driving at an unsafe speed, but no legal sanctions followed.

One of the Jupiter Island officers mentions that some media have arrived but are being kept at a far distance down the road. Woods, looking at his phone, mutters something like, “How ’bout all the drones over my house?” It’s not clear whether he’s talking about his general state of affairs or something he has been told is happening right now.
“I get 10 to 15 drones hovering over my back garden,” says Woods.
“At that point, what exactly are you looking for?” empathizes one of the other officers now on the scene, Lieutenant Rosko of the Martin County Sheriff’s Department.
“They have GoPros on them,” says Woods, as though he’d failed to make his point quite clear.
“Like, they looking to catch you in the pool or what?” says Rosko. “It’s like, come on.”
“I don’t know,” says Woods.

I come across no photos published from that day, but the New York Post will publish a drone image taken the following morning, its big exclusive being that, within a gated and fenced compound with sensors and security guards (though naturally they omit these details), Tiger Woods has carelessly left his front door half-open.

Four months after this accident took place, I am standing at the exact spot where Tiger Woods’s car came to rest. I know from all the footage I have seen that his vehicle left huge marks all over the road—wild wavy lines, presumably from when his tires were fighting but failing to keep their grip on the road, and the final dark smudges imprinted by the sliding side of his car. The kind of marks that linger for years on roads all over this country, echoes of dramas small and large that only the weather and passing traffic may slowly mute. That’s why I expected to see them here now.

But no. Jupiter Island (where the houses currently publicly listed on the market are priced between $5 million and $45 million) is clearly not that kind of place. There is no indication that this stretch of road has been resurfaced, but it seems to have been scrubbed with extraordinary care, and unless you know exactly where to look, and how to match the faint remaining traces to what was once there, you wouldn’t notice anything. It’s as though, as far as the world of Jupiter Island is concerned—and maybe as the world of Jupiter Island might prefer it—nothing ever happened here.

The Sheriff’s department says that the sheriff’s statement on the evening of the accident will be its only comment. The construction company whose employee helped Woods out of his car argues that company policy forbids its employee from speaking. When I drop around one afternoon to the house of Jeromy Bullard, who lives in a quiet neighborhood a few miles away, I can see the trailer Woods hit parked along the side of the house, but in response to my first ring of the doorbell, a generic recorded voice says, “Sorry! We’re not interested! Have a great day!” When I ring again, Bullard’s wife comes to the door. She’s perfectly friendly, but says that her husband is busy and that they’d rather not elaborate any further about what happened.

Woods stands up and strides down the empty drive toward the yacht club. (Though, according to chatter between the milling officers, “It’s the only yacht club in America without yachts. They [literally] don’t have a frickin’ dock. There’s a bar and a dining hall. They call it a yacht club.”)
Once Woods is some way down the drive, far away from anyone else, he can be seen striding back and forth, talking on the phone.
“Mr. Woods! Mr. Woods!” hollers Rosko, beginning to walk after him. Woods has strayed too far. “Mr. Woods!”
Woods keeps talking on the phone.
“I need to get you to come down here and hang out down here with us, please,” Rosko shouts.
Woods starts moving back toward the car, and as he gets closer, his side of the call can be heard on Rosko’s body-camera microphone: “Thank you so much…alright…you got it…alright…thank you…bye.”
Woods looks up at Rosko.
“Say again?” he says.
“Can I just keep you down here with us, please?” Rosko says.
“Yeah,” says Woods, and then he raises his right arm, the one holding his phone, up in the air, as if to show off the phone and emphasize what he’s about to say.
“I was just talking to the president….”

Woods and Trump have known each other for some time—they played a round together, for instance, in Jupiter during Trump’s first term, in 2017. After Woods’s 2019 Masters triumph, Donald Trump tweeted that he had spoken to Woods to congratulate him and that he would be awarding him the Presidential Medal of Freedom. Woods is also currently dating Vanessa Trump, Don Junior’s ex-wife and mother of five of the president’s grandchildren.

Later that day, when the president is asked about what has just happened to Woods, he says, “I feel so badly. He’s, uh, he’s got some difficulty. There was an accident and that’s all I know. Very close friend of mine. He’s an amazing person, amazing man. But, uh, some difficulty.” When someone shouts a follow-up question, he says, “We, uh…we don’t…I don’t want to talk about it.”
Back by the car, Woods takes some kind of circular container out of his right pocket, opens it, and moves his hand toward his mouth.
“Nothing in your mouth, please!” says Rosko. “Nothing in your mouth!”
But it’s too late.
A few moments later, Woods pulls out a thin tube, though this time he asks permission.
The answer is no.
“No, no Carmex,” says Rosko. “You don’t need lipstick.”
This sentence hangs in the air, until Rosko corrects himself.
“No, not lipstick. Lip balm.”

Woods, arms crossed, has a question: “So what’s the protocol so far?” He’s told that people are working to get the cars out of the road (Bullard’s trailer needs a new tire) and that the deputy doing the crash investigation will brief him in due course. Eventually, the car is successfully winched upright. Huge scratches and dents are visible down its left side, and the driver’s side window holds its smashed glass in place. Woods’s security guard gets in the back, crouching under the deployed airbags, trying to lower the back seats so that he can access the trunk where the precious clubs are. No success. “Everything’s fucking electronic,” he says.

Instead, one of the officers strides over with a metal bar and smashes the back window. The security man pushes Woods’s golf bag out through the opened space. There is Woods’s famous orange-and-white plush tiger head cover, a version of which has been shielding his driver since his amateur days.

For years, his mother would buy him a new one each year, with the words “Rak jak Mea” (“Love From Mom” in Thai) sewn into each, and an animatronic talking-puppet version of this head cover even appeared in a series of Woods Nike commercials in 2003 and 2004, bantering with Woods, the tiger’s dialogue voiced by Paul Giamatti; now it is being manhandled through the smashed back window of the car.
Once the golf bag is free of the car, one of the officers cutting himself in the process, McNamara receives it. He immediately takes out the putter.
“Is that the one?” Fusco asks him.
“Yeah,” says McNamara, taking off its head cover.
“Piece of history right there,” says Fusco.
McNamara points to the precise, circular wear mark that has formed on the putter’s face.
“Twenty-seven years,” McNamara says.

Not long after he moved to Jupiter Island, Woods opened a restaurant in mainland Jupiter. (No retail establishments of any kind are allowed on Jupiter Island itself.) I dine there for two nights in a row, wondering if there might be some sense of him there, but it feels elusive. The restaurant is a strange fusion of sports bar and fine dining establishment. There’s a $52 scallop risotto, a $74 center cut rib eye, and, by my count, 36 screens in total, 17 above the U-shaped bar and 19 elsewhere in the restaurant, all showing live feeds of sports coverage, none of which anyone seems to be watching. There’s also a small, almost perfunctory area where you can buy clothes and hats from the Sun Day Red clothing range (named after Woods’s habit of wearing red for the final round of a championship), as well as rings with Woods’s logo on them and a selection of cigars.

The check comes in a folder with the words “Cuisine Fit for a Champion” on the outside, which opens up into some kind of scorecard bearing the words “Bluejack National,” which lists a series of three-digit numbers for what are clearly 18 golf holes, with higher numbers for “Tiger” than for anyone else. I ask my waiter what it means, but they have no idea. Only later, googling, do I (sort of) work it out. In 2016, Bluejack National in Montgomery, Texas, was the first Tiger Woods–designed golf course to open. The digits are yardages. There’s a printed “handwritten” exhortation on the back to “Tally it up!”
Deputy Brenovil, the accident investigator, brings some paperwork over to the car where Woods is once again sitting. He has come to announce his conclusions.
“Unfortunately,” he tells Woods, “for the accident you are at fault.”
“Yep,” says Woods.
“And subsequently you are issued a citation for careless driving resulting in a crash,” Brenovil says.
“Okay.”

“It is a moving violation, so fine is going to be 163. Four points will be assessed on your driving record. You can pay it, you can pay it and do traffic school to take the points off, or you can contest it in court.”
“Okay.”
“Alright,” Brenovil concludes. “Any questions for me?”
“Zero,” says Woods, accepting the paperwork.

At this moment, Woods’s face is inscrutable, but it’s hard not to feel that, nearly two hours after he looked down at his phone and the world tipped from vertical to horizontal, Woods might believe that he is about to put this day’s unfortunateness behind him. A moment when he may imagine that, aside from little more than the payment of $163, there will be no further consequences.

If so, that moment passes quickly. As Brenovil takes his leave, he steps aside and introduces Woods to a female officer who has been waiting her turn on the grass behind him.
“I’m Deputy Levenar,” she tells him. “I’m with the Martin Country Sheriff’s office traffic DUI unit.”
“Yes, ma’am,” Woods replies.
“So Deputy Gedeon requested that I respond here,” she says. (Brenovil’s first name is Gedeon.)
“Yes, ma’am.”
“To conduct a DUI investigation on you,” says Levenar.
Woods looks like he’s about to say “Yes, ma’am” again, but, instead, he swallows a large hiccup.
“So,” asks Levenar, “are you willing to perform a few field sobriety exercises to [establish] that you’re safe to operate a vehicle?”
“Sure,” Woods replies. “What do you need?”
Is he already thinking of—or does he even remember—the last time?
Tiger Woods’s Second Great Automotive Disaster

I am standing by the side of the road on Military Trail, a few miles southwest of Jupiter Island, just south of its junction with Indian Creek Parkway. To my left is Admiral’s Cove golf club, and in the meridian are flowers marking a more recent disaster, the death of a 20-year-old man named Randall Ray Love III in a December 2024 traffic accident.

This is where, just after 2 a.m. on May 29, 2017, Officer Palladino found Woods asleep in his black Mercedes, phone in his lap, engine still running, right blinker blinking. The driver’s side front and rear rims were damaged, and their respective tires were flat. Though this conclusion was not spelled out in the subsequent police report, this damage clearly seemed consistent with Woods’s car having repeatedly ground against the curb as Woods fell asleep. The front bumper on the driver’s side was also damaged, there were some white scrapes and scuff marks on the rear bumper, and the passenger side taillight appeared to be out.
Sometime soon after Woods was found, and woken, a second law enforcement official, Officer Fandrey, asked him, “Where you coming from?”
“LA,” Woods replied.
“From where?” Fandrey asked again.
“LA,” Woods repeated.

Los Angeles is over two and a half thousand miles from here. So perhaps Fandrey was giving Woods the benefit of the doubt—allowing for the possibility that Woods was taking the question as an inquiry to where he grew up—when Fandrey rephrased what he had been asking:
“From LA? Okay. Where are you coming from right now?”
“Uh, back down to Orange County.”
“You’re headed down to Orange County?”
“Yeah.”
“Okay. Do you know where you’re at now?”
“Uh, I do not know.”

The subsequent sobriety tests are painful to watch, and to hear. Woods, slurring, appears unable to comprehend, never mind physically act upon, basic instructions. The worst moment comes after Woods is asked: “Do you know the English alphabet from A to Z?”
“Yes,” he replied.

“What’s your highest level of education?” “Sophomore in college,” Woods replied. So far so good. (Woods attended Stanford, majoring in economics for two years before bowing to the extraordinary inevitability of his professional golf career; before Woods played his first PGA round, he already had $60 million of endorsements.)
Out on Military Trail, Woods was now asked to put his feet together, close his eyes, tilt his head backward.
“And you’re going to recite the entire English alphabet in a slow non-rhythmic manner,” he was told. “Meaning you’re not going to sing it, okay? Do you understand the instructions?”
“I do,” Woods said.
“Okay,” said the officer. “What were the instructions?”
And that is where it all fell completely apart.
“Not to sing the national anthem backwards,” said Woods, with apparent confidence.
“Not to sing the national anthem backwards?” the officer repeated.
“Right,” Woods confirmed.

Woods had stated, when questioned, that he had earlier taken some medications, and at the jail, where he slumps against a wall, he consented to a urine test. When the results came back, detected in his system were hydrocodone and hydromorphone (both potent opioids), alprazolam and alpha-hydroxy alprazolam (the central ingredient and breakdown product of Xanax), zolpidem (the sedative found in Ambien), and delta-9-carboxy THC (the breakdown product from THC consumption).

By then Woods had already issued a statement apologizing for the events of that night. “I understand the severity of what I did and I take full responsibility for my actions” he said, crediting an “unexpected reaction to prescribed medications” and declaring, “I will do everything in my power to ensure this never happens again.” He subsequently checked into a treatment facility.

As a result of that night’s arrest, he was initially charged with reckless driving, driving under the influence, and improper stopping/standing/parking, but eventually, that October, was allowed to plead guilty only to the first charge and was sentenced to a year’s probation, attendance of DUI school, 50 hours of community service, and a payment of $543.50.
Levenar leads Woods over to her car, parked in the middle of South Beach Road.

(From Levenar’s subsequent report: “While speaking to Woods, I observed him sweating profusely. Woods’ movement was lethargic and slow…I observed Woods limping and stumbling to the right. Woods appeared to have a leg injury and had a compression sock over his right knee.”)
“Do you have a leg injury?” she asks him.
“Yes I do,” Woods replies.
“So besides your leg,” she asks, “do you have any medical conditions that I need to know about?”
“Um, I’ve had seven back operations,” he replies.
“Okay,” she says.
“Um, 20-something other operations on my leg….” he adds.
“When was your recent surgery?” she asks. “How long ago?”
“October of last year,” he says.
“Okay, are you able to walk, lift your leg with no issues, or do you have…?” she begins.
“I have a limp,” he interjects. “And my ankle’s fused.”
Levenar is the first to request that Woods remove his sunglasses.
(From her report: “I observed his eyes to be bloodshot and glassy, I observed his pupils to be extremely dilated.”)
She asks how much he has had to drink today, and he replies with confidence: “None.”
“Do you take any medications?” she continues.
“Um, I take a few, yes,” he answers, and at her request lists them.
(From her report: “Woods advised he takes medication for high blood pressure, cholesterol, ibuprofen, and Vicodin.”)
Woods confirms that he took all his meds this morning. Then the testing begins.
For the first test, he has to follow the movement of a pen she is holding with his eyes, without moving his head. His hiccups have now become so loud that he acknowledges, “I’ve got the hiccups.”
(From her report: “Horizontal Gaze Nystagmus: Woods continuously moved his head from side to side and had to be instructed several times to keep his head straight.”)

Next, Woods is asked to tilt his head back at a 45-degree angle and close his eyes, put his hands by his side, then bring his fingertips to the tip of his nose and then back. Again, he struggles to follow the precise instructions.
(From her report: “Finger to Nose: When he was told to begin, Woods tilted his head back but did not close his eyes and had to be reminded to do so.”)
The third exercise involves placing one palm face up, then face down on the other at increasing speed.

(From her report: “Palm Pat: I instructed Woods to begin, he counted out loud ‘one,’ ‘two,’ but did not make contact with his hands between each count. Woods did not increase in speed and had to be reminded to do so.”)
The final exercise had a chain of four linked tasks that Woods has to remember.

(From her report: “Hand Coordination: Woods did not remain in the starting position as instructed and demonstrated. While explaining and demonstrating the exercise, Woods began the exercise prior to my instructions.”)
With that, the testing was concluded.
(From her report: “Woods had hiccups during the entire investigation.”)

Those looking for insight into Woods might do well to start with his boats. A keen free diver and spearfisherman, he is known to have two. In 2004, he reportedly bought a 154-foot yacht for $20 million. His second is reportedly a custom-built 59-foot boat that cost around $3 million. What’s most telltale about them is the names he has chosen for them. The larger boat is named Privacy. The smaller, Solitude.

After finding evidence that suggests Solitude is often moored at the dock of his home, on the bay side of Jupiter Island, I wonder whether it’s possible to even glimpse it from a public place. The shoreline opposite the bay from his house is filled by private homes, but some of the land appears undeveloped. Leaving my car in a nearby state park, I hike along the highway in the summer heat, looking for a way in. Sandy trails head into the distance toward the water, every vacant piece of land is posted as National Wildlife Refuge, unauthorized entry prohibited.

What about via water? I wonder whether local fishing charters or nature cruises might sometimes pass that way. A search for such possibilities reveals that I have severely underestimated—or maybe overestimated—the world in which we live. Here is how, in part, the “Jupiter, Florida: Intracoastal Waterway Cruise” is pitched: “View the incredible estates of Jupiter Island from the water. See properties of Tiger Woods, Olivia Newton-John, Ralph Lauren, and many more. Watch for turtles, dolphins, and manatees as you cruise!”
“Understood,” Woods then replies, and he is guided into the back seat of the car, his handcuffed hands behind him. As the seatbelt is placed on him, he once again hiccups.

A few hours later, I’m heading north along the Intracoastal Waterway as our lively guide reels off famous names—Perry Como, Burt Reynolds, Rosie O’Donnell, Gary Player, Celine Dion, Venus Williams, Greg Norman—while occasionally pointing out a turtle.

In truth, not everything on the tour is quite as advertised—Olivia Newton-John’s property-owning days are, of course, past us (though byzantine tales are told of what she did own, including one home she supposedly left because it was haunted by the ghost of the general contractor who died in the primary bedroom), and the Ralph Lauren residence is only alleged to be his on account of the fact that he has been spotted there “and it really does fit his whole aesthetic”—but we do soon arrive a short swim’s distance from Woods’s property: “On this property you will find a golf course that’s 3.5 acres, because why not, as well as two pools and a tennis court.” You can see nothing of Woods’s house or grounds or mini golf course from the water, just a bank of greenery. “As for Woods himself,” the tour guide says, “I’ve been told that one time our cruise personally saw him out there on the dock—and as soon as we came around the corner, he quickly went away.”
And there it is.
Though its prow faces outward, so that the name can’t be seen, this is Solitude.
What happens next initially seems like it’s nothing more than a part of the sobriety test.

“Stand up for me,” Levenar requests, in the same tone of voice as before. “And then you’re going to face my car. Go ahead and place your hands behind your back. There you go. So, at this time, I do believe your normal faculties are impaired, okay? And you’re under the unknown substance. Okay?”
It’s at this moment, as she is talking, that she and Sheriff Thomas slip handcuffs onto Woods’s wrists.
“So at this time,” she continues, “you’re under arrest for a DUI.”
Woods half tries to turn his head.
“I’m being arrested?” he asks.
He sounds both weary and a little confused.
“Yes, sir,” she replies.
On the Intracoastal Waterway Cruise, Woods’s name is invoked for the first time long before the boat reaches his property, as the guide describes a home on the mainland side of the bay:

“Here’s another three-story home with a red tile roof, has two towers on top of it. That used to belong to Swedish golfer Jesper Parnevik. He had five PGA Tour wins. Because he was Swedish, he did put in a full spa and sauna into that house, as well as a 1,000-bottle wine cellar…and he introduced his Swedish nanny to another professional golfer. Does anyone know who that was…? Yes, Tiger Woods. Okay, so they did end up getting married, but that was the marriage that ended with a golf club to a car and a lot of other drama.”
That, at least, is one version of the story.
Tiger Woods’s First Great Automotive Disaster

November 27, 2009. Tiger Woods and his wife of five years, Elin Nordegren, Parnevik’s former nanny, were living near Orlando with their two young children. That week, Woods had been trying to batten down and refute emerging media stories of his infidelity; on the evening when everything finally exploded, after he had gone to sleep (variously reported as having taken either Vicodin or Ambien), his wife went through his phone, texted one of Woods’s lovers as though she were Woods, and, the infidelity soon confirmed both by a reply and a subsequent phone conversation, apparently woke and confronted Woods.

All that is undisputed about what happened next is that Woods left the house in his car in the early hours of the morning but traveled only a few yards, his car looping around on the nearby street before hitting a fire hydrant and then colliding with a tree. When rescue services arrived, he was unconscious, though after he was taken to the hospital, it was determined that his injuries were not serious.

The scale of the media storm that followed is hard to convey. Woods would appear in some form on the front page of the next 21 daily editions of the New York Post (one more, it was famously noted, than the aftermath of the 9/11 attacks), detailing each new tale of infidelity and each new stage in the unraveling of his marriage. One recurrent story involved his wife and a golf club: The scurrilous version suggested she had been attacking him in the departing vehicle, though the official version implies that she used the club to rescue him after the crash. In the first of several statements, Woods segued from a public apology for his behavior to pushing back against “the many false, unfounded and malicious rumors that are currently circulating,” and stating, “My wife, Elin, acted courageously when she saw I was hurt and in trouble. She was the first person to help me. Any other assertion is absolutely false.”

Images that circulated of his car after that night’s crash showed that among the shattered glass on the floor behind the driver’s seat was a book, John Gribben’s illustrated primer Get a Grip on Physics. On page 20, to illustrate the fact that Galileo had already intuited Newton’s First Law of Mechanics by rolling balls down a slope and realizing that, without friction, they might roll forever, there is a drawing of a golfer, driver raised up above his head, ready to strike a ball on the tee, with the caption: Who knows where this ball will end up.
Woods was given a citation for dangerous driving, docked four points on his license, and fined $164.

Thomas asks the handcuffed Woods to spread his legs and begins to search him. Out of Woods’s right pocket, Thomas removes a white circular tin, apparently the same one Woods took something from earlier. It’s an energy supplement named TRGT Focus, blue-raspberry flavor. According to the TRGT website, this is a “clean, nicotine-free pouch for steady, cognitive support that elevates output without overstimulation” and contains Alpha GPC, L-Theanine, L-Tyrosine, magnesium, and Huperzine A. TRGT is a company founded by Vince Whaley, a PGA Tour golfer.
When Thomas moves on to Woods’s left pocket, at first he finds some loose AirPods. Then, digging deeper, he brings out two white pills.
“That’s a Norco,” says Woods.
“Okay,” says Thomas, placing the pills into an open bag. (The pill markings, M367, confirm them as a combination of hydrocodone and acetaminophen.)
“Realize if you have something else, please tell us now,” Thomas says.
“I’ve got nothing else,” Woods tells him.

“Because it’s an automatic felony if you introduce any contraband into a correctional facility, okay?” says Thomas. As Thomas is speaking, Woods lets a long drool of spit fall from the center of his mouth to the ground between his feet and Levenar’s car.
“Understood,” Woods then replies, and he is guided into the back seat of the car, his handcuffed hands behind him. As the seatbelt is placed on him, he once again hiccups.
At the entrance of the jail, Levenar announces her cargo: “Adult male.” Inside, Woods agrees to a Breathalyzer test, which shows no alcohol level.
But he refuses a urine test.

Later that day, the head of the police department gave a press conference in which he announced that Woods had been charged with “DUI, with property damage, and refusal to submit to a lawful test,” suggesting that Woods had been “not trying to incriminate himself,” noting, “here is a Florida statute which he will be charged with for refusing to take that test, but we will never get definitive results as to what he was impaired on at the

text:
The emergency call alerting police to what might quite reasonably be labeled Tiger Woods’s Fourth Great Automotive Disaster came at 1:17 p.m. on March 27, 2026, from the super-high-end exclusively residential neighborhood of Florida’s Jupiter Island. An accident involving two vehicles had taken place on South Beach Road, the two-lane route running north-south up the thin barrier island’s center, separating homes on the bay from homes on the ocean.

In the aftermath of the day’s events, facing serious legal charges, Woods would issue a brief statement and enter a written plea of not guilty. Otherwise, he said nothing about the crash. His spokesperson did not respond to requests for comment, and his lawyer, when reached by GQ, said he does not discuss pending cases.

But the copious police body-camera footage from the scene plays out every strange, unexpected beat of that day’s aftermath. It offers a grippingly vivid glimpse of the remote life of one of the finest sportsmen we have ever known, whose cyclical downfalls and triumphant returns have, more times than almost seems possible, been punctuated by a moment when a police officer approaches his wrecked car.

1:23 p.m.
March 27, 2026

A black Range Rover lies on its side, blocking one lane of the road. Its rear-window wiper goes pointlessly back and forth, back and forth, under the hot midday sun. Officer Anthony Fusco of the Jupiter Island Public Safety Department, just arriving, asks a man standing in the road, whose blue shirt identifies him as an employee of a local construction company, whether anyone is still in the car.

“No…he’s out,” says the man. The construction worker pulled up here just after the accident happened and helped the Range Rover’s driver clamber out of the passenger side door, the one facing up to the sky.

“Who’s involved?” asks Fusco.

What Fusco seems to mean by this is: Which of the people now on the scene were involved in the crash? But the man in the road answers his question in a slightly different way.

To do so, he lowers his voice almost to a whisper.

“Tiger Woods,” he says.

Who knows exactly what carousel of thoughts this information brings to Officer Fusco’s mind? All we can know for sure are the first two words that escape from his mouth in response.

“Oh shit,” he says.

As often as the capsule tale of Tiger Woods’s first rise is repeated, it never becomes any less improbable. He appeared on television playing golf at the age of two, already a prodigy, having learned to play by watching his father in their California garage. Whether propelled or guided by his father, at every stage of his youth Woods appeared to be better than anyone had ever been before him. By the time he turned professional, at 20 years old, he was already one of the most famous people in the country.

Whatever pressure all that expectation placed upon him, he delivered. For the next decade, golf was his. By age 32, he had won 14 majors. There was but one obvious remaining target ahead of him to cement his eternal greatness: Jack Nicklaus’s record of 18 majors. But Woods was comfortably ahead of schedule—by the same age Nicklaus had won 11—and it was surely just a question of time.

As though life, even for the greatest of us, ever remains that straightforward.

1:24 p.m.

Tiger Woods, in a shimmering blue shirt, dark shorts, black cap, and mirrored sunglasses, is kneeling with his right leg on the grass on the side of the road, while Officer Christopher Trajbar, also from the Jupiter Island Public Safety Department, puts on disposable black gloves before carefully feeling his way up and down Woods’s back. Having seen Woods’s overturned car, a few feet away, Trajbar knows what to expect in accidents like these. In particular, to look for kinds of physical damage that the damaged may not yet have noticed. As Trajbar will later explain to a colleague: “I could have sworn there would have been glass or something in his back.”

But, to Trajbar’s surprise, there’s nothing. Woods has, in this way at least, been lucky.

Over in his car, Fusco is on the police radio, updating someone on the unexpected situation that has presented itself: “Hey—it’s Tiger. I just need you over here, just because of the sensitivity of it. He’s the one who rolled over.” Meanwhile, Trajbar walks a few yards southward down the road and approaches another man, this one standing by a truck, a trailer behind it. This is who, and what, Woods hit before his car turned onto its side. A horizontal sign running along the side of the trailer loudly advertises the man’s calling: JEROMY BULLARD’S CLEANING SERVICES. Soft Wash Roof Cleaning. Exterior Wall Cleaning. Driveway & Patio Cleaning. Paver & Deck Sealing.

“I was getting ready to turn….” Bullard begins, and explains what happened, an account he will relate multiple times over the next hour or so.

Bullard was driving north, heading for his next job at 281 South Beach Road. As he neared the home’s driveway, he put on his right turn signal and began to brake. But in his mirrors he could see a car on the road behind him, and as it came closer and closer, he realized that the car wasn’t slowing down. “He didn’t see me,” Bullard says, “and he just kept coming.” Bullard tried to pull over as far as he could, but it wasn’t enough. The right side of the fast-approaching car hit the driver’s side fender of his trailer (presumably because the car swerved, too late, at the very last minute). Continuing past him, the car pitched onto its side and slid along the road.

As the questions keep coming, Bullard answers them as best he can. Asked how fast Woods was driving, he replies that he can’t tell. “I mean, I don’t think it was crazy. It was normal speed. I just don’t know what was going on…he might have just not saw me. I don’t know. That’s the only thing I can think of.”

And what, he is asked, were your observations of him when he got out of the vehicle? (Bullard also helped Woods from his car.)

“He seemed okay….”

Apologetic, or…?

“I think he was just…he was like, ‘Oh shit.’ I think he was just flustered. He lives just down there. I know him…you know, I know who he is. I’m sure it’s”—Bullard offers a kind of half laugh—“not something that he just wanted to have happen. I didn’t want it to happen. Especially by him. You know? You know what I mean?”

1:27 p.m.

Officer Fusco arranges for Woods to sit in the back seat of a police car, a few yards down the driveway to Hobe Sound Yacht Club, so that he can be somewhat out of the way.

“Are you alright?” Fusco asks. “Are you in any pain?”

“No,” says Woods. “No. No pain.”

“No back pain? No neck pain?”

“No.”

“Knee?”

“Nope.”

“Nothing?” Fusco reconfirms.

It is only now that Woods offers what may come to be seen as an important clarification.

“Nothing unusual,” he says.

The single most obvious reason why, after 2008, Woods’s career faltered so badly relates to the daunting series of physical setbacks he faced: cartilage damage, torn ACL, pinched nerve, back spasms and pain, sciatica, scar tissue. Over the next decade, he would undergo four back surgeries and three knee surgeries (totaling five), and his career seemed a stuttering catalog of rehabs, comebacks, and setbacks. Some commentators wondered about his instinct to play through pain and his tendency to return too soon. Also about his drive to put on upper body mass, and his unusual choice to leverage his celebrity to train with Navy SEALs. But Woods, looking back, would argue that his injuries were simply the consequence of pushing his body so hard for so long to be the best: “That’s just the wear and tear of doing my sport, of just trying to push it to win everything I possibly can. To win every single tournament I played in, I would do everything I possibly could. Like any sport, there’s a cost to it. There’s a cost of doing business and, unfortunately, for sportsmen and sportswomen, injuries are a part of it.”

They hit him hard. By the end of 2017, Woods, who had once cumulatively topped the weekly golf rankings for over 10 years, dropped out of the top one thousand. Though he kept pushing, kept coming back to the tour, it seemed rational to believe that his time as a competitor at the highest level was all but over.

Woods at the 2019 Masters, his most recent major win.

Augusta National/Getty Images

2:12 p.m.

Not long after the first responders arrive, Woods is joined by two people from his world. One, wearing a green shirt with a Smith & Wesson logo on its back, is part of the security detail stationed at Woods’s home two miles down the road, though from the conversations he has with the local officers it’s clear that he previously used to be one of them. The second, in a blue-and-white striped shirt from Woods’s golfwear merchandise line, Sun Day Red, is Rob McNamara, vice president of Woods’s company, TGR Ventures, though law enforcement will refer to him as Woods’s manager. He and Woods have known each other since they both played junior golf, and he has worked with, and been friends with, Woods for a quarter of a century. Business aside, Woods has long trusted him as an adviser on the mechanics of Woods’s game.

When Fusco talks with McNamara about the tow truck on its way that will right, and then remove, Woods’s car, McNamara alerts him to one particular priority: “It’s just the clubs.”

“Yeah, no, I understand,” says Fusco. “Worth more than my house.”

“The putter’s worth more than all of our houses,” McNamara says.

A few minutes later a new figure on the scene, Sheriff Deputy Brenovil of the Martin County Sheriff’s Department, introduces himself to Woods and explains that he will be doing the accident investigation. He asks Woods what happened.

This is how Woods explains it: “Yeah, I was looking down at my phone, looked at changing stations, and next thing I was…boom!”

The strange thing about the way Woods says this is that there’s no apparent acknowledgment or sense that he fucked up. Maybe he considers it simply too obvious to state. But it’s also true that you could easily listen to him talking here and get the impression that what he’s actually saying is: I was looking at my phone and changing radio stations and all the normal things you do when you’re driving, and suddenly the world played an unfair trick on me.

After Brenovil concludes this first conversation and walks away, Fusco asks Woods: “Other than the clubs, is there anything else in there that you absolutely need at the moment?”

“No,” says Woods. “Just the sticks.”

“‘Just the sticks’—okay,” repeats Fusco. After some more chat back and forth, he asks, “Is that putter just the one you’ve taken with your career, or what?”

“Uh,” says Woods, “I’ve won 14 majors with it.”

“With that putter?” says Fusco.

“Yeah,” says Woods.

“Wow,” says Fusco. “They didn’t call you the GOAT for nothing, man.”

Woods doesn’t visibly react to this sentence, though it’s hard not to wonder whether what he heard loudest was the intended compliment or Fusco’s use of the past tense.

“That one club,” McNamara says. “There’s only one other club that’s won more majors than that individual club. Jack had one, like, 3-wood or something.” (Jack Nicklaus used the same MacGregor Tommy Armour 3-wood between 1958 and 1995, including during all of his 18 major titles.)

Fusco turns back to Woods.

“Are you golfing in the Masters this year?”

“Hoping to,” says Woods, evenly.

“Depends on y’all,” mutters the green-shirted security man.

In the long decade after Woods’s 14th major victory, in 2008, as he kept coming back, kept trying, it was as though he believed something was possible that few other people did. Thing is, he was right. Improbably, after everything, in April 2019, his game having cohered for a while and his body holding together, he achieved one further triumph: winning the Masters, his 15th major. Coming off the 18th green, after one final stroke with that famous putter (this its 14th victory, because his very first had been with another), one of the first people he hugged after his family was McNamara.

And Woods is trying, still. He never explicitly states where he was heading in the car today before this accident, but the circumstantial evidence suggests he was off to the golf course. His clubs are in the car; the local golf course he has been known to play at, Medalist, is in the direction he was going; and at one point today, as they wait, he says to McNamara, “So much for hitting balls today.”

Three days earlier, Woods had played for his Jupiter Links team in the new TGL team golf league he has been an instrumental part of creating: a format which uses a hybrid of a golf simulator for long shots and real putting surfaces. It was the first true competitive game of any kind Woods had played since the previous February, his most recent surgeries having been for a ruptured left Achilles tendon in March 2025 and a disc replacement surgery on his spine that October. Nonetheless, in the press conference after Jupiter Links’ loss that night, when Woods was asked whether he might play in the Masters, only two weeks away, he’d made clear that he wasn’t yet ruling it out.

“I’ve been trying,” he said. “This body, it doesn’t recover like it was when I was 24, 25. It doesn’t mean I’m not trying. I’ve been trying for a while…I keep trying. I want to play…I’ll be practicing playing at home this week, and keep trying to make progress.”

That, presumably, is what today, until things went wrong, was for. He was trying. By now, though, he was dealing with more than just the physical damage caused by all his years of golf.

Tiger’s Car Crash Timeline

Woods has a history of dangerous incidents while behind the wheel. None led to death or injuries, save the ones that Woods sustained.

Tiger Woods’s Third Great Automotive Disaster

On February 22, 2021, Tiger Woods was playing golf at Rolling Hills Country Club, just south of Los Angeles, a course he hadn’t returned to since his junior golf tournament days. (When, naturally, he had won; the prize back then was a boom box.) After the 2019 Masters win, Woods’s career had resumed its stop-start trajectory—a fifth knee operation, then a brief hot streak going into 2020 before his body had once more rebelled. Now Woods was nursing himself back into competitive form after his fifth back operation, a microdiscectomy, though that day he was being filmed by Friday Night Lights director Peter Berg as he offered golfing instruction to three celebrities: Dwyane Wade, David Spade, and Jada Pinkett-Smith.

In return, Pinkett-Smith in particular—who told him she started taking golf seriously in 2019 after her husband called and told her to turn the TV on during the final round of the Masters because “Tiger’s about to make history”—got him to open up a little.

At one point, when he seemed to be implying that he just can’t do everything in quite the same way as he once could, and then said, “Sucks when you’re older,” she pushed back.

“I like the wisdom that comes with it,” she said.

“Yeah, but…” he retorted.

“The body?” she asked.

“But the body…” he said.

A while later, when he picked up this thought—“You’re right about the wisdom part of it but…the body. I’ve had 10 operations”—she countered by telling him that it’s so inspiring what he’s overcome. Woods seemed bemused and embarrassed by this.

“I just don’t look at it like that,” he said.

“Well, you should,” she told him.

“But I don’t know how to,” he responded.

“Tiger,” she said, “your journey has been absolutely amazing.”

“Hmmm,” he said.

“It has been amazing,” she repeated.

“I just don’t see it that way,” Woods said.

“One day you will,” she told him.

“I don’t think so,” he said. He was smiling, almost bashful, but shaking his head. “I don’t look at it like that.”

“You should,” she persisted.

“I know,” he said. “I just look at the fight.”

This didn’t sound like banter. It sounded as though, caught off guard by someone he respected, Woods couldn’t think of anything to say but the truth.

They shared one more particularly noteworthy exchange, as they walked across the course down toward a lake. Pinkett-Smith explained that golf is a new kind of challenge for her because she’s never been a particularly disciplined person and she’s never had to work that hard at much.

“You feel like you’ve, like, have gotten away with just talent?” asked Woods.

“Yes,” she said.

“For me,” he said, “I always thought I wasn’t the most talented. So I felt like I had to work my ass off. Because I was always younger than everyone else…so I wanted to become, like, better…. I was always small…I wasn’t, like, the best at what I did.”

It’s a mesmerizing exchange. In part, for Woods’s demeanor, more honest and thoughtful and real than the stilted, awkward, punchier persona he often presents to the world. But it is also fascinating for the context it offers to what would happen next. When things go wrong in Tiger Woods’s world—and they were once more about to do so—such events are sometimes depicted as evidence that Woods has long been lost in an unsafe, self-destructive hazy spiral. Even if there are ways in which that might be so, this taping with Pinkett-Smith is a snapshot of how Woods was only hours before it all went wrong again: open, lucid, vulnerable, and in all obvious ways, entirely together.

The next morning, Woods was due back at Rolling Hills for more filming. New celebrity tutees, Drew Brees and Justin Herbert, would be waiting. Just before seven o’clock, Woods picked up his car from the valet at the Terranea Resort where he was staying and headed off. Just over halfway to his destination, as he drove down Hawthorne Boulevard, his Genesis SUV failed to follow the curve of the road. Instead, it, and Woods, traveled straight on, first hitting the central meridian and smashing through the large wooden sign announcing “Welcome to Rolling Hills Estates,” then crossing the two lanes of traffic in the opposite direction, before plowing into shrubbery, uprooting a tree, and finally coming to rest on its side. The car’s inbuilt event-data-recorder system would suggest that his vehicle had been traveling at over 80 miles an hour (the speed limit was 45) and offered no indication that the brakes were applied before the crash.

The first person on the scene, a local resident, found Woods unconscious. Deputy Carlos Gonzalez of the LA County Sheriff’s office, who arrived soon afterward, observed that Woods’s vehicle had “massive front end damage” and later told the news media: “I’ve seen fatal traffic collisions, so I will say it’s very fortunate that Mr. Woods was able to come out of this.”

In the trauma bay at Harbor-UCLA hospital, a police investigator interviewed Woods (referred to in his report as P-1): “P-1 told me he did not remember being involved in a traffic collision. P-1 thought he was currently in the state of Florida.” As the investigator and Woods spoke, a deep laceration on the right side of his jaw was being stitched, but it was his leg and foot injuries that were far more serious. The surgeon soon offered an update: “Comminuted open fractures affecting both the upper and lower portions of the tibia and fibula bones were stabilized by inserting a rod into the tibia. Additional injuries to the bones of the foot and ankle were stabilized with a combination of screws and pins. Trauma to the muscle and soft tissue of the leg required surgical release of the covering of the muscles to relieve pressure due to swelling.”

Amputation, Woods revealed eight months later, had been on the table. He spent three weeks in the hospital and more than two more months at home in Jupiter Island in a hospital bed. He talked about what a milestone it was when he could first be wheeled outdoors in the Florida sun, and how he eventually could use crutches. “I’d built a really nice house,” he observed, “but I didn’t realize how big it was until you start putting crutches on.”

When interviewed on the day of the crash, Woods denied having drunk alcohol or taken prescription medication either the previous night or that morning, and no testing was done which contradicted his assertions. The police report offered the opinion that Woods was at fault for driving at an unsafe speed, but no legal sanctions followed.

2:38 p.m.
March 27, 2026

One of the Jupiter Island officers mentions that some media have arrived but are being kept at a far distance down the road. Woods, looking at his phone, mutters something like, “How ’bout all the drones over my house?” It’s not clear whether he’s talking about his general state of affairs or something he has been told is happening right now.

“I get 10 to 15 drones hovering over my back garden,” says Woods.

“At that point, what exactly are you looking for?” empathizes one of the other officers now on the scene, Lieutenant Rosko of the Martin County Sheriff’s Department.

“They have GoPros on them,” says Woods, as though he’d failed to make his point quite clear.

“Like, they looking to catch you in the pool or what?” says Rosko. “It’s like, come on.”

“I don’t know,” says Woods.

I come across no photos published from that day, but the New York Post will publish a drone image taken the following morning, its big exclusive being that, within a gated and fenced compound with sensors and security guards (though naturally they omit these details), Tiger Woods has carelessly left his front door half-open.

Four months after this accident took place, I am standing at the exact spot where Tiger Woods’s car came to rest. I know from all the footage I have seen that his vehicle left huge marks all over the road—wild wavy lines, presumably from when his tires were fighting but failing to keep their grip on the road, and the final dark smudges imprinted by the sliding side of his car. The kind of marks that linger for years on roads all over this country, echoes of dramas small and large that only the weather and passing traffic may slowly mute. That’s why I expected to see them here now.

But no. Jupiter Island (where the houses currently publicly listed on the market are priced between $5 million and $45 million) is clearly not that kind of place. There is no indication that this stretch of road has been resurfaced, but it seems to have been scrubbed with extraordinary care, and unless you know exactly where to look, and how to match the faint remaining traces to what was once there, you wouldn’t notice anything. It’s as though, as far as the world of Jupiter Island is concerned—and maybe as the world of Jupiter Island might prefer it—nothing ever happened here.

The Sheriff’s department says that the sheriff’s statement on the evening of the accident will be its only comment. The construction company whose employee helped Woods out of his car argues that company policy forbids its employee from speaking. When I drop around one afternoon to the house of Jeromy Bullard, who lives in a quiet neighborhood a few miles away, I can see the trailer Woods hit parked along the side of the house, but in response to my first ring of the doorbell, a generic recorded voice says, “Sorry! We’re not interested! Have a great day!” When I ring again, Bullard’s wife comes to the door. She’s perfectly friendly, but says that her husband is busy and that they’d rather not elaborate any further about what happened.

2:43 p.m.

Woods stands up and strides down the empty drive toward the yacht club. (Though, according to chatter between the milling officers, “It’s the only yacht club in America without yachts. They [literally] don’t have a frickin’ dock. There’s a bar and a dining hall. They call it a yacht club.”)

Once Woods is some way down the drive, far away from anyone else, he can be seen striding back and forth, talking on the phone.

“Mr. Woods! Mr. Woods!” hollers Rosko, beginning to walk after him. Woods has strayed too far. “Mr. Woods!”

Woods keeps talking on the phone.

“I need to get you to come down here and hang out down here with us, please,” Rosko shouts.

Woods starts moving back toward the car, and as he gets closer, his side of the call can be heard on Rosko’s body-camera microphone: “Thank you so much…alright…you got it…alright…thank you…bye.”

Woods looks up at Rosko.

“Say again?” he says.

“Can I just keep you down here with us, please?” Rosko says.

“Yeah,” says Woods, and then he raises his right arm, the one holding his phone, up in the air, as if to show off the phone and emphasize what he’s about to say.

“I was just talking to the president….”

Woods and Trump have known each other for some time—they played a round together, for instance, in Jupiter during Trump’s first term, in 2017. After Woods’s 2019 Masters triumph, Donald Trump tweeted that he had spoken to Woods to congratulate him and that he would be awarding him the Presidential Medal of Freedom. Woods is also currently dating Vanessa Trump, Don Junior’s ex-wife and mother of five of the president’s grandchildren.

Later that day, when the president is asked about what has just happened to Woods, he says, “I feel so badly. He’s, uh, he’s got some difficulty. There was an accident and that’s all I know. Very close friend of mine. He’s an amazing person, amazing man. But, uh, some difficulty.” When someone shouts a follow-up question, he says, “We, uh…we don’t…I don’t want to talk about it.”

2:51 p.m.

Back by the car, Woods takes some kind of circular container out of his right pocket, opens it, and moves his hand toward his mouth.

“Nothing in your mouth, please!” says Rosko. “Nothing in your mouth!”

But it’s too late.

A few moments later, Woods pulls out a thin tube, though this time he asks permission.

The answer is no.

“No, no Carmex,” says Rosko. “You don’t need lipstick.”

This sentence hangs in the air, until Rosko corrects himself.

“No, not lipstick. Lip balm.”

Woods, arms crossed, has a question: “So what’s the protocol so far?” He’s told that people are working to get the cars out of the road (Bullard’s trailer needs a new tire) and that the deputy doing the crash investigation will brief him in due course. Eventually, the car is successfully winched upright. Huge scratches and dents are visible down its left side, and the driver’s side window holds its smashed glass in place. Woods’s security guard gets in the back, crouching under the deployed airbags, trying to lower the back seats so that he can access the trunk where the precious clubs are. No success. “Everything’s fucking electronic,” he says.

Instead, one of the officers strides over with a metal bar and smashes the back window. The security man pushes Woods’s golf bag out through the opened space. There is Woods’s famous orange-and-white plush tiger head cover, a version of which has been shielding his driver since his amateur days.

For years, his mother would buy him a new one each year, with the words “Rak jak Mea” (“Love From Mom” in Thai) sewn into each, and an animatronic talking-puppet version of this head cover even appeared in a series of Woods Nike commercials in 2003 and 2004, bantering with Woods, the tiger’s dialogue voiced by Paul Giamatti; now it is being manhandled through the smashed back window of the car.

Once the golf bag is free of the car, one of the officers cutting himself in the process, McNamara receives it. He immediately takes out the putter.

“Is that the one?” Fusco asks him.

“Yeah,” says McNamara, taking off its head cover.

“Piece of history right there,” says Fusco.

McNamara points to the precise, circular wear mark that has formed on the putter’s face.

“Twenty-seven years,” McNamara says.

Not long after he moved to Jupiter Island, Woods opened a restaurant in mainland Jupiter. (No retail establishments of any kind are allowed on Jupiter Island itself.) I dine there for two nights in a row, wondering if there might be some sense of him there, but it feels elusive. The restaurant is a strange fusion of sports bar and fine dining establishment. There’s a $52 scallop risotto, a $74 center cut rib eye, and, by my count, 36 screens in total, 17 above the U-shaped bar and 19 elsewhere in the restaurant, all showing live feeds of sports coverage, none of which anyone seems to be watching. There’s also a small, almost perfunctory area where you can buy clothes and hats from the Sun Day Red clothing range (named after Woods’s habit of wearing red for the final round of a championship), as well as rings with Woods’s logo on them and a selection of cigars.

The check comes in a folder with the words “Cuisine Fit for a Champion” on the outside, which opens up into some kind of scorecard bearing the words “Bluejack National,” which lists a series of three-digit numbers for what are clearly 18 golf holes, with higher numbers for “Tiger” than for anyone else. I ask my waiter what it means, but they have no idea. Only later, googling, do I (sort of) work it out. In 2016, Bluejack National in Montgomery, Texas, was the first Tiger Woods–designed golf course to open. The digits are yardages. There’s a printed “handwritten” exhortation on the back to “Tally it up!”

“Unfortunately,” he tells Woods, “for the accident you are at fault.”

“Yep,” says Woods.

“And subsequently you are issued a citation for careless driving resulting in a crash,” Brenovil says.

“Okay.”

“It is a moving violation, so fine is going to be 163. Four points will be assessed on your driving record. You can pay it, you can pay it and do traffic school to take the points off, or you can contest it in court.”

“Okay.”

“Zero,” says Woods, accepting the paperwork.
